title: @EventListener, @TransactionalEventListener, ApplicationEventPublisher
prerequisites: Understanding of transactions and loose coupling

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A hotel has a bell that announces 'a guest checked in'. Anyone interested can sign up to hear the bell: the housekeeping crew hears it and prepares the room; the billing desk hears it and opens the account. The people who signed up don't need to know each other — they just react to the bell. The bell also has a special rule: the billing desk can ask to be rung only AFTER the check-in paperwork is fully recorded (after transaction commit), so it never acts on half-finished paperwork. If the paperwork fails, the desk is never rung at all.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Spring events decouple components: publish with ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(order)); listen with @EventListener on a method: @EventListener public void on(OrderPlacedEvent e) { ... }. The listener runs synchronously by default in the publisher's thread. For async, add @Async to the listener (and @EnableAsync). @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) runs the listener only after the transaction commits — perfect for sending emails/notifications that should not happen if the transaction rolls back. @TransactionalEventListener has a fallbackExecution attribute to also run when there is no transaction.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Spring's event mechanism is a simple observer pattern within the ApplicationContext: publishEvent notifies the ApplicationEventMulticaster, which dispatches to registered ApplicationListener beans (or @EventListener-annotated methods adapted into ApplicationListenerMethodAdapter). By default the multicaster (SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster) invokes listeners synchronously in the caller's thread — an exception in a listener propagates to the publisher (unless configured otherwise). @Async listeners run on the application's async executor, decoupling timing and adding failure isolation. @TransactionalEventListener is a special listener registered with a transaction phase: the TransactionSynchronization triggers it after commit/rollback/completion, so the listener sees committed data.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent resolves the event to a payload type and calls the multicaster's multicastEvent. SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster looks up listener beans and invokes each listener's onApplicationEvent (or the adapted @EventListener method, resolving the event argument). With @Async, the multicaster's taskExecutor (ThreadPoolTaskExecutor) runs the invocation asynchronously. @TransactionalEventListener registers the listener with a TransactionSynchronization via TransactionSynchronizationManager: on commit, the afterCommit synchronization invokes the listener; if the transaction rolls back and phase=AFTER_ROLLBACK, it runs then; fallbackExecution controls behavior with no active transaction. Event inheritance and generics resolution (ResolvableType) determine which listeners match which events.

codeComparison.title: Direct service-to-service calls vs events
codeComparison.summary: Calling another service directly couples the components and runs regardless of transaction outcome; events decouple them and can wait for commit.

legacyOrBad.label: Direct call in the same transaction

modernOrGood.label: Publish event + transactional listener

interviewGotchas.question: Why should side effects like emails use @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) instead of a plain @EventListener?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the transaction-aware event model — interviewers want the commit/rollback semantics that prevent acting on data that never materialized.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: A plain @EventListener runs synchronously at publish time, which is INSIDE the transaction (if the publisher method is @Transactional). If the transaction later rolls back, the listener has already acted on data that no longer exists — an email sent for an order that was never committed. @TransactionalEventListener with phase AFTER_COMMIT registers the listener to be invoked by the transaction synchronization AFTER the commit succeeds: the listener runs only when the data is durable, and it does NOT run at all if the transaction rolls back (unless you also use AFTER_ROLLBACK or fallbackExecution). This guarantees side effects are consistent with committed state. The trade-off: the listener runs later (after commit), so it can't affect the transaction, and the commit must succeed for it to fire.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is '@TransactionalEventListener just delays the listener'. It binds the listener to the transaction outcome — no commit, no callback (for AFTER_COMMIT). Another trap: assuming the listener shares the transaction — after commit, the transaction is gone, so the listener starts its own (or none); data read in the listener sees the committed state. Candidates who explain the synchronization binding show real Spring event mastery.

interviewGotchas.question: What happens if a listener throws, and how does async vs sync execution change the behavior?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the failure semantics — interviewers want to know whether an exception in a listener affects the publisher/transaction and what async execution changes.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: With the default synchronous multicaster, a listener exception propagates back to the publisher (publishEvent) — so if a @EventListener throws, the exception bubbles into the publishing method and can roll back its transaction (if @Transactional). This is often surprising: a failing notification listener can break the core operation. With @Async listeners, the invocation happens on the async executor thread, so the exception does NOT propagate to the publisher — the core flow is isolated, but the failure is silent unless you handle it in the listener or a global async exception handler (AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler). @TransactionalEventListener exceptions: after commit, an exception propagates from the afterCommit callback, which can cause an error at the transaction boundary. Best practice: make listeners resilient (catch and log, or retry) so a notification failure never corrupts the primary transaction.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'listener exceptions are isolated'. Synchronous listeners propagate exceptions to the publisher. Another trap: assuming async listeners' failures are logged by default — unhandled async exceptions vanish unless you register an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. Candidates who distinguish the sync-propagation and async-isolation paths show real understanding.
